title: Enums vs Literal Unions
summary: See why Node can't run an enum, and replace it with literal unions and as const objects that keep the names callers use.
intro: Many TypeScript codebases use `enum` for a fixed set of values, like statuses or log levels. Node runs TypeScript by erasing the types, and an enum isn't only a type: it also creates an object when the program runs. This lesson shows what an enum does, the erasable patterns that replace it, and how to move existing code off enums.

steps.title: What enums are
steps.body:
`enum Level { Low, Medium, High }` declares a type, and it also creates a real object at runtime. Numeric members count up from 0, so `Level.Low` is 0, and the object maps back the other way as well: `Level[0]` is `"Low"`. A string enum like `enum Status { Active = "active" }` gives each member its value and has no reverse mapping.

That generated object is why an enum isn't erasable. Deleting the types would delete the object too, and every `Level.Low` would break. So Node refuses enums, and the course config's `erasableSyntaxOnly` makes `tsc` refuse them as well, with TS1294. `const enum` is refused the same way.

What an enum stands for is a plain object, and a plain object runs anywhere:

```typescript
const Level = { Low: 0, Medium: 1, High: 2 } as const;
console.log(Level.Medium); // 1
```

Add a type with the same name, and the object can stand in for the enum both as a value and as a type.

examples.title: A numeric enum
examples.prompt: Declare a numeric enum and print a member and its name, with the course config's checker on.
examples.output: main.ts(1,6): error TS1294: This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled.
examples.explanation: The checker points at the enum's name, on line 1 at column 6, and the program never runs. A compiler that emits JavaScript, with `erasableSyntaxOnly` off, would turn the enum into an object, and the file would print `1` for `Level.Medium`, then `High` for `Level[Level.High]`, the reverse mapping from 2 back to its name. Example 3 prints the same two lines without an enum.

examples.title: What Node does with an enum
examples.prompt: Turn the checker off with `// @ts-nocheck` and let Node run the same enum.
examples.errorIncludes: SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode
examples.explanation: `// @ts-nocheck` switches type checking off for the file, so `tsc` reports nothing. Node then strips the types, finds the enum, and stops with `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX` before running a single line, which is why nothing prints. Stripping only ever deletes type syntax and never writes new code, and an enum needs new code. A project that still has enums runs through `tsx` or a `tsc` build, which turn them into JavaScript first.

examples.title: The same thing as plain data
examples.prompt: Replace the enum with an `as const` object and a type of the same name, and print the same two values.
examples.explanation: `as const` keeps each value as a literal (`Level.Medium` has the type `1`, not `number`) and makes the object readonly. `(typeof Level)[keyof typeof Level]` is the union of its values, as the bubble shows. Giving that type the same name lets `Level` work in both places an enum did: as an annotation in `level: Level`, and as an object in `Level.High`. There is no reverse mapping, so `levelName` looks the name up itself with a `switch`.

practice.title: Replace an enum
practice.prompt:
The starter declares a string enum, which the course config refuses with TS1294. Replace it so the file type-checks and prints the same lines the enum would.

1. Turn `enum Status` into an exported `as const` object named `Status`, with the same names and values.
2. Export a type named `Status` too, the union of the object's values.
3. Leave the code that uses `Status.Active` and `Status.Archived` as it is.

Expected output:

```text
Website: active
Old blog: archived
Mobile app: active
Active projects: 2
```

tests.output:
Website: active
Old blog: archived
Mobile app: active
Active projects: 2

cases.name: Status works as a type and as a value
Status only allows its own values

hints: Example 3 does the same for numbers: an object with `as const`, then a type of the same name built from it.
The object keeps the enum's names and values, written as properties: `Active: "active"` and `Archived: "archived"`.
`export type Status = (typeof Status)[keyof typeof Status];` is the type. Then `status: Status` and `Status.Active` both compile again.

steps.title: Literal unions and as const objects

examples.title: A plain union
examples.prompt: Sort tasks by priority, with an `as const` array for the order and a union derived from it.
examples.output:
high: Fix login bug
medium: Review PR
low: Update docs
examples.explanation: `LEVELS` holds the values in the order you wrote them, and `(typeof LEVELS)[number]` turns them into the union. The bubble lists the members in the checker's own order, since a union has no order, so the order lives in `LEVELS`. `LEVELS.indexOf(...)` ranks each priority, from 0 for low up to 2 for high. Subtracting `a`'s rank from `b`'s sorts high first, and `toSorted` returns a new array, leaving `tasks` as it was.

examples.title: Same name for value and type
examples.prompt: Use `Color.Red` the way you would use an enum member, with an `as const` object and a type of the same name.
examples.explanation: `Color.Green` is just the string `"green"`, so that is what prints. `hex` takes a `Color`, the union of the three strings, so it accepts `Color.Red` and the plain string `"blue"` alike. A string enum would reject `hex("blue")` with TS2345, because an enum member isn't interchangeable with its string. That difference makes literal unions easier to use across a codebase, in tests, and in JSON. The `switch` covers every member, so no `return` is needed after it.

examples.title: What changes for callers
examples.prompt: See what callers get from a string union: readable JSON, the same exhaustive switch, and a list of the values.
examples.explanation: With a numeric enum, this ticket would serialize as `{"id":7,"priority":2}`, and anyone reading the JSON, a log, or a database row would have to know what 2 means. A string value explains itself. The `never` check works exactly as it does for discriminated unions: add a member to `Priority` and `responseHours` stops compiling until it has a case. `Object.values` lists the values in the order you wrote them, which is handy for menus and validation, and when you type a `Priority`, the editor offers the three strings as completions.

practice.title: Log levels
practice.prompt:
Turn the starter's log levels into an `as const` object with a type of the same name, then decide which messages get logged.

1. Add `as const` to the exported `LogLevel` object.
2. Replace `type LogLevel = string` with the union of the object's values, exported under the same name.
3. Make `shouldLog(level, min)` return `true` when `level` comes at or after `min` in `ORDER`, which runs from debug to error.
4. Check also calls `shouldLog` with other levels.

Expected output:

```text
debug at min info: false
info at min info: true
error at min warn: true
warn at min error: false
```

tests.output:
debug at min info: false
info at min info: true
error at min warn: true
warn at min error: false

debug at min info: false
info at min info: true
error at min warn: true
warn at min error: false
error at min debug: true
debug at min debug: true
info at min warn: false

cases.name: accepts a member and a plain string
keeps each value as a literal

hints: `as const` goes right after the object's closing brace. The type is `(typeof LogLevel)[keyof typeof LogLevel]`, as in the colors example.
`ORDER.indexOf(level)` is a level's position: 0 for debug up to 3 for error.
Return `ORDER.indexOf(level) >= ORDER.indexOf(min)`: a message is logged when its level is at least as severe as the minimum.

steps.title: Moving code off enums
steps.body:
A migration keeps the names callers already use, so most code only changes where the enum is declared: it becomes an `as const` object and a type of the same name. Three patterns cover the rest.

- **Bit flags.** Powers of two become an `as const` object of numbers. `|` (bitwise OR) combines flags into one number, and `&` (bitwise AND) tests whether a flag is in it.
- **Strings from outside.** Input and JSON arrive as `string`, so a type guard checks them against the list of values first.
- **Reverse lookups.** Code that read a name back with `Level[2]` finds it with `Object.entries` instead.

```typescript
const Flag = { A: 1, B: 2 } as const;
const both = Flag.A | Flag.B;
console.log(both, (both & Flag.B) !== 0); // 3 true
```

Skip `const enum` too. The compiler pastes its values into the code that uses it, so it needs a compiler just as `enum` does, and this config refuses it with TS1294. Under `isolatedModules`, which compiles one file at a time the way Node does, a `const enum` from a library is an error too (TS2748). You'll still meet enums in older codebases and in frameworks like Angular and NestJS, which build with a compiler. Code that can't migrate yet runs with `tsx`, as a later lesson shows.

examples.title: Bit flags
examples.prompt: Combine permissions into one number with `|`, and test them with `&`.
examples.output:
editor mask: 3
editor can write: true
viewer can delete: false
admin can delete: true
examples.explanation: Each flag is its own bit: 1 is binary 001, 2 is 010, and 4 is 100. `Permission.Read | Permission.Write` turns on both bits, giving 3 (011). `perms & p` keeps only the bits both numbers have, so it is non-zero exactly when `p`'s bit is on. A combined value like 3 is a plain `number` and not one of the flags, so the single flags get a type of their own, `PermissionValue`, while `can` takes the combination as `perms: number`.

examples.title: Parsing into a union
examples.prompt: Check strings from standard input against the list of levels before using them as a `Level`.
examples.output:
ok: high
ok: low
not a level: urgent
ok: medium

examples.title: Reverse lookup
examples.prompt: Find the name of a status code, the way an enum's reverse mapping did.
examples.explanation: A numeric enum maps values back to names, so `HttpStatus[404]` gave `"NotFound"`. An `as const` object only maps names to values. `Object.entries` lists its `[name, value]` pairs, and `find` returns the first pair whose value matches, or `undefined` when none does. `statusName` takes any `number` because codes arrive from outside, and 418 isn't in the object, so it prints `Unknown`.

practice.title: Permissions
practice.prompt:
Store a user's permissions as bit flags in a single number.

1. Make the exported `PermissionValue` type the union of `Permission`'s values.
2. Make `grant(perms, p)` return `perms` with `p`'s bit turned on, using `|`.
3. Make `has(perms, p)` return whether `p`'s bit is on in `perms`, using `&`.
4. Check also calls `grant` and `has` with other flags.

Expected output:

```text
read: true
write: false
delete: true
mask: 5
```

tests.output:
read: true
write: false
delete: true
mask: 5

read: true
write: false
delete: true
mask: 5
all three: 7
writer can read: false
7 can write: true

cases.name: rejects a combined mask as one flag
rejects a flag that doesn't exist
returns the new mask as a number

hints: `PermissionValue` is built the same way as in the bit flags example: `(typeof Permission)[keyof typeof Permission]`.
`perms | p` turns on `p`'s bit and keeps every bit that was already on.
`(perms & p) !== 0` is `true` exactly when `p`'s bit is on in `perms`.

recap:
- An `enum` creates an object at runtime, so it isn't erasable: `tsc` refuses it with TS1294 under `erasableSyntaxOnly`, and Node with `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`.
- A union of string literals is the simplest replacement. Keep the values in an `as const` array and derive the type with `(typeof LEVELS)[number]`.
- For names like `Color.Red`, pair an `as const` object with `type Color = (typeof Color)[keyof typeof Color]`.
- Literal unions accept plain strings, serialize readably, and work with exhaustive `never` checks.
- Bit flags become `as const` numbers, combined with `|` and tested with `&`.
- Check strings from outside with a type guard before using them as the union, and look names up with `Object.entries`.
- `const enum` needs a compiler too. `tsx` runs code that can't migrate yet.
